title: How a Falling Cat Flips With Nothing to Push On
description:
A falling cat has nothing to push against, and a body falling with no spin can't start spinning on its own. So how does it flip? It bends in the middle and twists its front and back halves against each other, tucking and stretching its legs. Total spin stays zero, and it still lands feet down.

First photographed in 1894, explained with maths in 1969. Kittens start doing it at 3 to 4 weeks old.

Sources:
- T. R. Kane and M. P. Scher, 'A dynamical explanation of the falling cat phenomenon', International Journal of Solids and Structures 5(7), 663-670 (1969). doi:10.1016/0020-7683(69)90086-9
- E.-J. Marey, 'Des mouvements que certains animaux exécutent pour retomber sur leurs pieds lorsqu'ils sont précipités d'un lieu élevé', Comptes Rendus 119, 714-717 (1894).
- G. J. Gbur, Falling Felines and Fundamental Physics, Yale University Press (2019).
- J. A. Sechzer et al., 'Development and maturation of postural reflexes in normal kittens', Experimental Neurology 86(3), 493-505 (1984).

How it's made: original 3D characters and scenes, animated by us. No cats were dropped. The voices are AI voices (ElevenLabs).

Counterphysical: cat physics that breaks your intuition.
